articles.title: How to add wallets to your app with an API
articles.excerpt: On Lit Protocol you can add a wallet to your app with six REST calls and no SDK. You create a wallet, create a group, write a signing rule, connect them, make an API key for your server, and sign. The…
articles.body: On Lit Protocol you can add a wallet to your app with six REST calls and no SDK. You create a wallet, create a group, write a signing rule, connect them, make an API key for your server, and sign. The key is created and stored inside a secure enclave. The rule that decides when it signs is a JavaScript function that runs in the same enclave. The record of which rules can use which wallets is stored on Base. I will walk through the six calls, and then say a little about when Lit is the right choice and when it is not. The six calls Go to the Lit dashboard and click Create an account . Choose API key , fill in your email and an account name, and copy the account API key it gives you. The base URL for everything below is https://api.chipotle.litprotocol.com/core/v1 . First, create a wallet.

articles.title: How to Tailor Your Resume to a Job Without Lying
articles.excerpt: Tailoring means choosing, ordering and naming real experience. Here is where it ends and invention begins. Almost every piece of job-search advice says to tailor the resume to the job. Very little of…
articles.body: Tailoring means choosing, ordering and naming real experience. Here is where it ends and invention begins. Almost every piece of job-search advice says to tailor the resume to the job. Very little of it explains where tailoring stops and making things up starts. With AI writing tools a click away, that line matters more than it used to, because a tool asked to "match this job post" will happily add skills, titles and results that never happened. A resume that claims experience the candidate does not have can sometimes get through a first screen. It rarely survives the conversation that follows. One question about a tool that was never used, or a result that cannot be explained, and the rest of the resume loses its credibility too. The good news is that honest tailoring is not complicated.

The next application round opens November 23, 2026 . But that headline needs context: the new round awards 50,000 grants, each covering the applicant and up to two collaborators. articles.title: Vector Search vs Web Search for Insurance Claims Intake: Audit Logs and Freshness
articles.excerpt: Insurance claims intake is a retrieval problem with a clock attached. A claim answer can be semantically relevant and still be wrong if the policy amendment landed yesterday, or if an adjuster cannot…
articles.body: Insurance claims intake is a retrieval problem with a clock attached. A claim answer can be semantically relevant and still be wrong if the policy amendment landed yesterday, or if an adjuster cannot show which document supported the answer. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. Keep vector search for the claim corpus, use web search only for approved external material, and make freshness plus audit fields part of the retrieval contract before picking a vendor. The incident lesson: relevance is not the whole answer I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries.

articles.body: TL;DR what: The FBI issued a FLASH advisory warning that multiple threat actors have used ARTEX, an AI-driven autonomous penetration testing framework, to automate cyberattacks worldwide since at least August 2026. impact: ARTEX was used in the ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain attack, which hit at least 162 Microsoft 365 tenants and targeted more than 2,250, and in attacks on South Korean financial institutions that exposed data on about 67,000 people. fix: There is no patch because ARTEX is an attack tool; the FBI's 13-page advisory includes IOCs and hardening guidance, and MalwareMustDie has released an open-source detection signature pack and a confidence-graded detection playbook.

articles.title: How to compress a JPG to an exact KB size in the browser (and why 50 KB is two numbers)
articles.excerpt: Exam, visa and job application forms love hard limits: "photo under 50 KB", "signature between 10 and 20 KB". A canvas can export a JPEG at any quality you like, but there is no toBlob(..., { maxBytes…
articles.body: Exam, visa and job application forms love hard limits: "photo under 50 KB", "signature between 10 and 20 KB". A canvas can export a JPEG at any quality you like, but there is no toBlob(..., { maxBytes: 50000 }) . So you have to search for the right settings. Here is the search I ended up with, and the small details that decide whether the portal accepts the file. First: "50 KB" means two different numbers Some sites count 1 KB as 1,000 bytes, some as 1,024. A file has to pass both readings, so: a maximum is converted with 1,000 (the smaller number): "under 100 KB" means at most 100,000 bytes a minimum is converted with 1,024 (the larger number): "at least 20 KB" means at least 20,480 bytes export const maxKbToBytes = ( kb : number ) => Math .

articles.title: Judge Me by My Size, Do You? What Your Viewport Really Costs an AI Tester
articles.excerpt: Yoda told Luke that size matters not. With all due respect to the little green guy, he never had to pay for a computer-use agent's screenshots. Here's how I ended up down this rabbit hole. I recently…
articles.body: Yoda told Luke that size matters not. With all due respect to the little green guy, he never had to pay for a computer-use agent's screenshots. Here's how I ended up down this rabbit hole. I recently pointed Claude at a web app to do some functional testing, and my usage went way up. My gut said screenshots were the culprit: the agent has to look at the screen before nearly every move, and every look costs tokens. So my tongue-in-cheek pitch for a blog post became "monitor size actually matters for AI-driven testing." But talk is cheap, so I had a small team of AI agents build and run an experiment to prove or disprove it. Let's see what happened. Spoiler: size matters, just not in the direction you'd guess every time. The Math You Can Do on a Napkin Claude doesn't see pixels.

articles.title: What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 is approaching a distance of one light-day from Earth, a milestone that highlights the enormous distances involved in deep-space exploration.
articles.body: After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth. This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond. Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA.

articles.title: Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger
articles.excerpt: A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to feder…
articles.body: A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged. Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and says it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data . more…

articles.title: 'Maybe the scariest thing I've heard in my life': Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover reveals his toughest challenge before flying to the moon
articles.excerpt: For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, one of the hardest parts of traveling to the moon happened before he even left Earth.
articles.body: TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Former NASA astronaut Victor Glover has flown in combat, performed four spacewalks and strapped himself to the top of rockets launching into space. But before embarking on his historic Artemis II journey around the moon, he faced something even more difficult: a conversation with his four daughters. Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet. "This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover said.
